units.text: INT. PYGMALION - CONTINUOUS
Covent Garden at 11.15 p.m.
Torrents of heavy summer rain.
Cab whistles blowing frantically in all directions.
Pedestrians running for shelter into the market and under the portico of St. Paul’s Church, where there are already several people, among them a lady and her daughter in evening dress.
They are all peering out gloomily at the rain, except one man with his back turned to the rest, who seems wholly preoccupied with a notebook in which he is writing busily.
The church clock strikes the first quarter.
THE DAUGHTER [in the space between the central pillars, close to the one on her left] I’m getting chilled to the bone.
What can Freddy be doing all this time?
He’s been gone twenty minutes.
THE MOTHER [on her daughter’s right] Not so long.
But he ought to have got us a cab by this.
A BYSTANDER [on the lady’s right] He won’t get no cab not until half-past eleven, missus, when they come back after dropping their theatre fares.
But we must have a cab. We can’t stand here until half-past eleven. It’s too bad.
units.name: THE MOTHER

units.text: Well, it ain’t my fault, missus.
units.name: THE BYSTANDER

units.text: If Freddy had a bit of gumption, he would have got one at the theatre door.
units.name: THE DAUGHTER

units.text: What could he have done, poor boy?
units.name: THE MOTHER

units.text: Other people got cabs. Why couldn’t he?
units.name: THE DAUGHTER

units.text: Freddy rushes in out of the rain from the Southampton Street side, and comes between them closing a dripping umbrella.
He is a young man of twenty, in evening dress, very wet around the ankles.
Well, haven’t you got a cab?
units.name: THE DAUGHTER

units.text: There’s not one to be had for love or money.
units.name: FREDDY

units.text: Oh, Freddy, there must be one. You can’t have tried.
units.name: THE MOTHER

units.text: It’s too tiresome. Do you expect us to go and get one ourselves?
units.name: THE DAUGHTER

units.text: I tell you they’re all engaged. The rain was so sudden: nobody was prepared; and everybody had to take a cab. I’ve been to Charing Cross one way and nearly to Ludgate Circus the other; and they were all engaged.
units.name: FREDDY

units.text: Did you try Trafalgar Square?
units.name: THE MOTHER

units.text: There wasn’t one at Trafalgar Square.
units.name: FREDDY

units.text: Did you try?
units.name: THE DAUGHTER

units.text: I tried as far as Charing Cross Station. Did you expect me to walk to Hammersmith?
units.name: FREDDY

units.text: You haven’t tried at all.
units.name: THE DAUGHTER

units.text: You really are very helpless, Freddy. Go again; and don’t come back until you have found a cab.
units.name: THE MOTHER

units.text: I shall simply get soaked for nothing.
units.name: FREDDY

units.text: And what about us? Are we to stay here all night in this draught, with next to nothing on. You selfish pig—
units.name: THE DAUGHTER

units.text: Oh, very well: I’ll go, I’ll go.
units.name: FREDDY

units.text: He opens his umbrella and dashes off Strandwards, but comes into collision with a flower girl, who is hurrying in for shelter, knocking her basket out of her hands.
A blinding flash of lightning, followed instantly by a rattling peal of thunder, orchestrates the incident.
Nah then, Freddy: look wh’ y’ gowin, deah.
units.name: THE FLOWER GIRL

units.text: Sorry
units.name: FREDDY

units.text: he rushes off.
THE FLOWER GIRL [picking up her scattered flowers and replacing them in the basket] There’s menners f’ yer!
Te-oo banches o voylets trod into the mad. [She sits down on the plinth of the column, sorting her flowers, on the lady’s right.
She is not at all an attractive person.
She is perhaps eighteen, perhaps twenty, hardly older.
She wears a little sailor hat of black straw that has long been exposed to the dust and soot of London and has seldom if ever been brushed.
Her hair needs washing rather badly: its mousy color can hardly be natural.
She wears a shoddy black coat that reaches nearly to her knees and is shaped to her waist.
She has a brown skirt with a coarse apron.
Her boots are much the worse for wear.
She is no doubt as clean as she can afford to be; but compared to the ladies she is very dirty.
Her features are no worse than theirs; but their condition leaves something to be desired; and she needs the services of a dentist].
How do you know that my son’s name is Freddy, pray?
units.name: THE MOTHER

units.text: Ow, eez ye-ooa san, is e? Wal, fewd dan y’ de-ooty bawmz a mather should, eed now bettern to spawl a pore gel’s flahrzn than ran awy atbaht pyin. Will ye-oo py me f’them?
units.name: THE FLOWER GIRL

units.text: Here, with apologies, this desperate attempt to represent her dialect without a phonetic alphabet must be abandoned as unintelligible outside London.
Do nothing of the sort, mother. The idea!
units.name: THE DAUGHTER

units.text: Please allow me, Clara. Have you any pennies?
units.name: THE MOTHER

units.text: No. I’ve nothing smaller than sixpence.
units.name: THE DAUGHTER

units.text: THE FLOWER GIRL [hopefully] I can give you change for a tanner, kind lady.
THE MOTHER [to Clara] Give it to me. [Clara parts reluctantly].
Now [to the girl] This is for your flowers.
Thank you kindly, lady.
units.name: THE FLOWER GIRL

units.text: Make her give you the change. These things are only a penny a bunch.
units.name: THE DAUGHTER

units.text: Do hold your tongue, Clara.
units.name: THE MOTHER

units.text: To the girl.
You can keep the change.
units.name: THE MOTHER

units.text: Oh, thank you, lady.
units.name: THE FLOWER GIRL

units.text: Now tell me how you know that young gentleman’s name.
units.name: THE MOTHER
